title: Transpiration
tagline: Transpiration as water vapour loss, stomatal, lenticular and cuticular types, the potometer, factors affecting rate and the significance of transpiration.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, and it is closely linked to the movement of water through the plant. This chapter defines transpiration, distinguishes the three types, describes the potometer as a tool for estimating the rate, explains the factors that increase or decrease the rate, and discusses why transpiration matters to a plant even though it is a continuous loss of water.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts, mainly through stomata

facts.label: Measurement
facts.value: Potometer estimates the rate by measuring water uptake

facts.label: Factors
facts.value: Light, temperature, humidity, wind and surface area

blocks.text: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant. It is not the same as the simple evaporation from a wet surface, because in a plant the water must leave through special structures and the process is linked to the opening and closing of stomata. The three types are stomatal transpiration, lenticular transpiration and cuticular transpiration. Stomatal transpiration occurs through the stomata and is the largest part of water loss in most leaves. Lenticular transpiration occurs through the lenticels of stems and branches, and cuticular transpiration occurs through the cuticle of the leaf and stem. In a healthy green leaf, stomatal transpiration is by far the most important.

items: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from aerial parts.
It happens mainly through stomata.
The three types are stomatal, lenticular and cuticular.
Stomatal transpiration is the largest in most leaves.
Cuticular transpiration is less when the cuticle is thick.
Lenticular transpiration occurs in woody stems and branches.

items.text: Most of the water lost from a green leaf leaves through the stomata, usually on the lower surface.
items.note: Stomatal transpiration is the main route because stomata are the main openings to the air.

items.text: A woody twig loses some water through lenticels, especially when the bark is young and permeable.
items.note: Lenticular transpiration is usually small compared with stomatal transpiration.

blocks.text: A potometer is an instrument used to estimate the rate of transpiration by measuring the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot. A leafy shoot is cut under water, fitted to a capillary tube with a reservoir, and as the shoot transpires, water is drawn up and an air bubble moves along the tube. The distance moved by the bubble in a given time gives an estimate of the rate. The potometer measures uptake, which is taken as an approximation of transpiration. This assumption is not perfect, because some water is used in photosynthesis and retained in growth, so uptake slightly overestimates loss. The potometer is best used for comparisons, such as light versus shade, rather than for measuring the absolute amount of water lost.

items.meaning: Instrument that estimates transpiration by measuring water uptake of a cut shoot.
In potometry, that water uptake approximately equals water loss by transpiration.
A comparison of rates under two conditions using the same shoot or similar shoots.

items: A potometer measures water uptake, which is used as an estimate of transpiration.
The shoot is cut under water to prevent an air lock in the xylem.
An air bubble is used to track movement of water in the capillary tube.
The assumption is that uptake approximately equals transpiration.
Uptake slightly overestimates loss because some water is used in photosynthesis and growth.
The potometer is best for comparisons between conditions.

items.text: A potometer may show that a shoot in bright light takes up water faster than the same shoot in shade.
items.note: This demonstrates the effect of light on transpiration.

items.text: A leafless shoot or a shoot with fewer leaves usually shows a slower rate because there is less surface area for transpiration.
items.note: Surface area is one of the factors affecting the rate.

learn.title: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration

blocks.text: The rate of transpiration is affected by several environmental and internal factors. Light is a major factor because it opens the stomata and is also associated with warming. Temperature increases the rate because warmer air holds more water vapour and increases evaporation. Humidity decreases the rate because if the outside air is already moist, the gradient between the leaf and the atmosphere is smaller. Wind increases the rate because it removes the layer of moist air around the leaf, steepening the gradient. Surface area affects the total loss, because more leaf area means more stomata and more evaporation. Internal factors such as the number and distribution of stomata, the thickness of the cuticle and the plant's water supply also matter.

items.meaning: A factor that increases transpiration mainly by opening stomata.
A factor that increases transpiration by increasing evaporation and the water-holding capacity of air.
A factor that decreases transpiration when high, because it reduces the water-vapour gradient.
A factor that increases transpiration by removing the moist boundary layer from the leaf.
The exposed leaf area, which influences the total amount of transpiration.

items: Light increases transpiration mainly by opening stomata.
Temperature increases transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration.
Wind increases transpiration by removing moist air from the leaf surface.
More surface area increases the total amount of transpiration.
Internal factors such as stomatal number and cuticle thickness also affect the rate.

items.text: A plant in hot, dry, windy weather transpires faster than the same plant in cool, humid, still air.
items.note: Several factors can work together to raise or lower the rate.

items.text: A plant with small, thick leaves loses less water by cuticular transpiration than a plant with large, thin leaves.
items.note: Adaptations of the leaf affect the rate in addition to the environment.

blocks.text: Transpiration is often described as a necessary evil because it causes a great loss of water, but it also has important effects. First, it generates the transpiration pull that helps pull water and dissolved minerals up the xylem from the roots. Second, it helps cool the leaves because evaporation removes heat. Third, it helps keep the plant tissues moving and keeps water flowing so that materials can be transported. Its cost is also real: in dry or hot conditions the plant may lose water faster than it can replace it, and then wilting can occur. Plants therefore need a water supply, and some are adapted to reduce transpiration when water is scarce.

items.meaning: Suction force generated by water loss that helps draw water up the plant.
Cooling effect produced when water evaporates from a surface.
A process that is costly but also useful and hard to do without.

items: Transpiration helps pull water and minerals up the plant.
It has a cooling effect on the leaves.
It keeps water moving through the plant.
It causes a continuous loss of water, which is its main disadvantage.
It may cause wilting if water loss exceeds water uptake.
Plants may adapt to reduce transpiration in dry conditions.

items.text: A tall tree depends on the transpiration pull to move water to its highest leaves.
items.note: Transpiration is one of the main drivers of the water column in tall plants.

items.text: A plant in drought may close its stomata to reduce transpiration, but then it also takes in less carbon dioxide.
items.note: Reducing transpiration can restrict photosynthesis, showing the trade-off.

assessment.title: Transpiration: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the types, instruments, factors or functions clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention water vapour, aerial parts and stomata.

exercises.prompt: Name the three types of transpiration.
exercises.answer: The three types are stomatal transpiration, lenticular transpiration and cuticular transpiration.
exercises.explanation: All three types should be named.

exercises.answer: A potometer is an instrument used to estimate the rate of transpiration by measuring the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention the rate of water uptake and the estimation of transpiration.

exercises.prompt: State two factors that increase transpiration.
exercises.answer: Light and temperature increase transpiration; wind also increases transpiration.
exercises.explanation: Any two of light, temperature or wind carry the marks; humidity is the main factor that decreases it.

exercises.prompt: How does humidity affect the rate of transpiration?
exercises.answer: High humidity decreases the rate of transpiration because the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air becomes smaller, so water vapour diffuses out more slowly.
exercises.explanation: The answer should mention the gradient and the slower rate.

exercises.prompt: Why is transpiration called a necessary evil?
exercises.answer: Transpiration is called a necessary evil because it causes a continuous and often large loss of water, but it is also useful because it helps pull water and minerals up the plant, cools the leaves and keeps water moving through the tissues.
exercises.explanation: The answer should mention both the loss of water and the useful functions.

questions.prompt: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of:
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from aerial parts of the plant.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing liquid water — that is guttation, not transpiration.

questions.explanation: Most transpiration occurs through the stomata.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing hydathodes — those are associated with guttation, not transpiration.

options: Water uptake as an estimate of transpiration
questions.answer: Water uptake as an estimate of transpiration
questions.explanation: A potometer measures water uptake and uses it as an estimate of transpiration.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing water lost exactly — the potometer measures uptake, not loss directly.

questions.prompt: Which factor decreases the rate of transpiration?
questions.explanation: High humidity decreases the rate of transpiration by reducing the water-vapour gradient.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing wind — that usually increases the rate.

questions.prompt: Which factor increases transpiration mainly by opening stomata?
questions.explanation: Light increases transpiration mainly by opening the stomata.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing humidity — that usually decreases transpiration.

questions.prompt: Which type of transpiration is the largest in a healthy green leaf?
questions.explanation: Stomatal transpiration is the largest in most healthy green leaves.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing cuticular — that is usually a smaller part of total transpiration.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: transpiration helps pull water up the plant by creating a ________.
questions.explanation: The pulling force generated by transpiration is called transpiration pull.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'root pressure' — that is a push from below, not the pull from above.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a potometer measures water ________ as an estimate of transpiration.
questions.explanation: A potometer measures water uptake and uses it as an estimate of transpiration.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'loss' — the apparatus measures uptake, not loss directly.

questions.prompt: Describe the potometer and state its assumption.
questions.answer: A potometer is an instrument used to estimate transpiration by measuring the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot. The shoot is cut under water and fitted to a capillary tube; an air bubble is used to track water movement, and the distance moved in a given time gives an estimate of the rate. The assumption is that the rate of water uptake is approximately equal to the rate of transpiration.
questions.explanation: A good answer describes the apparatus, the bubble method and the assumption.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the potometer measures water lost exactly — it measures uptake as an approximation.

questions.prompt: State how light, temperature and humidity affect transpiration.
questions.answer: Light increases transpiration mainly by opening the stomata. Temperature increases transpiration by increasing evaporation and the water-holding capacity of the air. Humidity decreases transpiration by reducing the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the air, so water vapour diffuses out more slowly.
questions.explanation: The answer should give the effect and a brief reason for each factor.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that one increases and the other decreases without giving the reason.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of transpiration and state its disadvantages.
questions.answer: Significance: transpiration generates the transpiration pull that helps draw water and dissolved minerals up the xylem from the roots; it has a cooling effect on the leaves due to evaporation; and it helps maintain the flow of water through the plant. Disadvantages: transpiration causes a continuous loss of water, which is a cost to the plant; in dry or hot conditions it may cause wilting if water loss exceeds uptake; and reducing transpiration, as by closing stomata, can also reduce carbon dioxide uptake and photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: A full answer should give the pull, the cooling effect and the flow effect, and the main disadvantages.
questions.commonMistake: Only listing the loss of water without explaining why transpiration is still important.

questions.prompt: A plant in a closed, humid room transpires more slowly than the same plant in a dry, windy room. Explain why.
questions.answer: In the closed, humid room the air outside the leaf is already moist, so the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the air is small and water vapour diffuses out slowly. If the room is also quiet, the moist layer of air around the leaf is not removed, which also reduces the rate. In the dry, windy room the air is drier and the wind removes the moist boundary layer, so the gradient is steeper and transpiration is faster. Thus humidity and wind together explain the difference.
questions.explanation: The answer should link humidity to the gradient and wind to the removal of moist air.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the plant 'feels' the wind — the explanation should refer to the boundary layer and gradient.
